extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of literature and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and extracting normative and rhetorical principles from Montaigne's Essays (Renaissance personal/philosophical essays). Focuses on Montaigne's claims about virtue, fortune, custom, religion, and civic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: True victory
rubrics_metrics.description: A true victory consists in compelling the conquered, in mind and will, to admit they are conquered; external force alone is not a complete victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted maxim: “Victoria nulla est, Quam quae confessor animo quoque subjugat hostes.” Example: Hungarians content themselves with extracting a confession or oath and then release prisoners; the moral is that psychological/substantive submission is the mark of victory, not mere physical domination or ransom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour as stability of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Valour is not bodily strength, good arms, or the advantages of fortune, but steadiness of courage and will — constancy of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Leonidas and his men at Thermopylae, Captain Iscolas choosing glorious death over safety. 'Valour is stability, not of legs and arms, but of the courage and the soul.' The honour of valour lies in fighting steadfastly, not merely in prevailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between being killed and being conquered
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who dies obstinately and maintains courage to the last is killed by fortune but not conquered by the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sign of true greatness: one who dies with defiance (e.g., fighting on his knees) is not defeated in the moral sense. 'He is killed, not conquered.' This evaluates heroism by inner constancy rather than outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy under terror as true courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining cheerfulness, defiance, and composure under threats and imminent death demonstrates genuine courage and moral victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed behavior of certain prisoners who, despite being threatened with horrific deaths, remain merry, taunt captors, and sing defiant songs (even joking that executioners eat their ancestors). Montaigne presents this as superior to mere physical survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural relativism in marital customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs that appear monstrous to one culture (e.g., many wives equating to honour) may be virtuous within another's standards; do not judge solely by one's own norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne defends polygamous practice in the foreign people by comparing it to Biblical examples (Sarah, Leah, Rachel) and historical instances (Livia, Stratonice). The guidance is to recognize and weigh other cultural logics rather than reflexive condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposture thrives on ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters unknown or abstruse furnish fertile ground for imposture; the less people know, the more readily they accept extravagant claims about gods or occult practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Plato's observation that it is easier to satisfy hearers about gods than men; alchemists, judicial astrologers, fortune-tellers, and quacks exploit ignorance. The practical principle is to be skeptical of confident claims made about the unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not validate religion by worldly success
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not attempt to prove or shore up religious truth by appealing to the prosperity or success of earthly enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that attributing divine approval to military or political success misleads the vulgar and risks undermining faith when fortunes reverse (examples: wars and shifting outcomes such as Rochelabeille, Moncontour, Jarnac). Religion should rest on sounder foundations than transient events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the inscrutability of divine will
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enough to believe that events come from God and to receive them with acknowledgment of divine wisdom; human reason should not presume to fully discern God's counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions against those who 'interpret and control the designs of God' and attempt to assign causes to every event. Scriptural and patristic references (Book of Wisdom, St. Augustine) underline the prudence of humble acceptance over presumptuous explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject using chance events as theological proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing specific divine motives to particular coincidences or deaths (e.g., the sudden deaths of controversial figures) is unreliable and often absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes the folly of constructing theological judgments from accidental resemblances (e.g., comparing deaths of Arius and Pope Leo, Heliogabalus, Irenaeus). Practical advice: avoid over-interpreting singular events as moral verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune's reasoned unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune often acts in ways that resemble reasoned artifice — producing results surprising or opposite to human designs — and may sometimes better human prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative stories: poisoned wine accidentally killed the father rather than the intended target; Protogenes' ruined painting improved by a sponge strike; Jason cured by a battle wound; examples of providential redirection (Isabel of England). The principle: expect variability and occasional 'better' outcomes beyond calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic provision for mutual advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: A public municipal office or place should exist in every city where people can post and learn of mutual needs (jobs, trades, servants, buyers/sellers), improving public correspondence and reducing needless want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts his father's proposal: an officer to enter and mediate requests (e.g., pearls buyers/sellers, servants, artisans). Benefits: helps notable poor scholars, connects supply and demand, prevents ignorance of others' needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household journal-keeping for memory and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a household journal (besides daily accounts) recording remarkable occurrences, visits, travels, changes of servants, marriages, deaths, and principal events to preserve memory and resolve disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne's father's rule: steward keeps a journal as a lasting memorial useful for recalling beginnings/ends of things and settling uncertainties. He commends revival of this custom and admits personal neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish custom from natural law in clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothing practices are primarily customs rather than strict natural necessities; what is 'natural' about dress should be judged by broader polity and comparative observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments/examples: some peoples go naked in similar or colder climates; natural covering of animals suggests humans originally were adequately 'clothed'; Plato's health advice (minimal head/feet coverings); examples of leaders and peoples with varied clothing habits (Egyptians, Persians, Poles, King of Mexico). Use comparative evidence rather than assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging others by oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not commit the common error of evaluating others solely by one's own habits or preferences; be open to many ways of life and admit difference rather than demand uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explicitly rejects imposing his own form of life on others: 'I easily believe that in another’s humour which is contrary to my own.' This is a general tolerance principle for moral and cultural judgment.
